item.title: Scientists Discovered a Mysterious Lost Human Species
item.author: Becky Ferreira
item.content:encoded: Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that reconnected with old relatives, broke the quasar frontier, went deep, and worked on their cores.First, scientists unearth teeth in China that belonged to an unidentified lineage of humans that lived 100,000 years ago. Then: a new cosmic distance record, DEEP-SEA EXPLOSIVE VOLCANISM, and a swim in alien seas. Scientists have discovered a mysterious human lineage that lived in China 100,000 years ago and does not appear to belong to known species such as Neanderthals, Denisovans, or our own group, In other words: this could be a completely new type of human, unknown to science.Modern humans are the sole survivors of what was once a diverse group of apes in the genus, known as hominins. The last of our known fellow humans, Neanderthals and Denisovans, went extinct about 40,000 and 30,000 years ago, respectively. This sprawling family tree of extinct humans raises the question of how many of our cousins walked our planet but left few traces. This is especially true in warm humid climates that aren’t conducive to fossilization, such as southern China. But despite the long odds, researchers have discovered several hominin teeth in two cave sites, Chuanshandong and Longchuandong, in the subtropical Guangxi region.The Longchuandong cave teeth likely belonged to Denisovans, a lineage that split from Neanderthals about 400,000 years ago. The Chuanshandong teeth were another story, however. By studying the shape and preserved proteins in the teeth, the team found that they don’t match up with any known hominin, suggesting they could belong to a new form of extinct archaic human. “The scarcity of hominin fossils from subtropical southern China during the Middle to Late Pleistocene transition has hampered our understanding of the geographical distribution of Denisovans and the potential existence of other lineages in mainland East Asia,” said a team co-led by researchers based in China and Spain.“The findings of this study show that the subtropical area in southern China may have hosted multiple populations of archaic during the Middle and Late Pleistocene,” the team concluded. “In addition to the previously suggested Neanderthal-related hominin at Maba in the adjacent Guangdong Province, we have now identified both a Denisovan-affinity hominin and another unresolved non-sapiens archaic in this region.”The team cautioned that the find is still “preliminary” and it will take more fossils and research to determine the identity of the Chuanshandong hominin, including whether it belongs to a known lineage, such as , or is a novel species. Regardless, it’s clear that there is much more to learn about our long-lost cousins, and why we are the only one left among them. A blast from the very, very, very distant pastMeet Dún Aonghasa, the most distant quasar ever glimpsed by humans. Since peering deep into space is also a way of looking back in time, this quasar—a type of ultra-radiant galactic core—is from a region where the universe was only 630 million years old. Quasars are extremely energetic galactic cores that barf out more continuous light than anything in the universe. Dún Aonghasa, officially known as J1504+6252, is the first quasar ever spotted beyond a “redshift” of 8, which is a measurement that correlates to light shifting into the red end of the spectrum as it travels across immense stretches of time and space before reaching Earth. The quasar was spotted by Europe’s Euclid telescope, and the discovery pushes “the quasar redshift frontier [back] by 39 million years, or approximately 6 percent of the age of the Universe at that epoch,” said researchers led by Julien Wolf of the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy, as part of the wider Euclid Consortium. The quasar is named after a prehistoric cliff-top fort in Ireland “where land gives way to a vast oceanic horizon to the west,” the team said. “Dún Aonghasa evokes both a boundary and an invitation: an apparent end at the edge of the cliff, with much still hidden beyond it. Likewise, J1504+6252 stands at the current observational frontier of quasars, illuminating the threshold to even earlier times still waiting to be explored.”Bonus points to the team for getting all poetic about it, though it raises the bar for whoever finds an even more distant quasar. You can’t just call it “Tom” or whatever—we expect lyrical metaphors in our quasar names now. We will move now from the most distant reaches of the universe to the deepest abyss in Earth’s oceans. It’s just that kind of week! Extending to nearly 6.8 miles under the Pacific Ocean, Challenger Deep is the deepest region in the seas, which makes it a tantalizing destination for submersible exploration (occasionally starring James Cameron). In late 2024, scientists were remotely exploring a trenchwall in the Challenger Deep forearc segment (CHFS) with the uncrewed vehicle when they discovered pyroclastic rocks forged by volcanism. Even though these volcanic layers were found at a shallower depth of 3.7 miles, they still represent the deepest known evidence of explosive volcanic activity ever found in the ocean. “A significant discovery includes the recovery of the deepest known pyroclastic deposits” at 6,000 meters or 3.7 miles “providing evidence for a distinct style of deep-sea explosive volcanism,” said researchers led by Robert J. Stern, professor emeritus at the University of Texas at Dallas.“These findings suggest the CDFS is a tectonically unstable and magmatically active zone, offering critical insights into the nature of the upper mantle, the behavior of volatile-rich magmas erupted at high pressure, and why the Challenger Deep is so deep,” the team said.Since is only equipped to venture to depths of 3.7 miles, the team floated the idea of crews following these volcanic breadcrumbs further into the abyss with ”ultra-deep” submersibles. Explosive volcanism may extend much deeper than currently known, for those brave enough to risk awakening Cthulhu.Journey to the center of EnceladusLife thrives at Challenger Deep, but could it also exist in extraterrestrial oceans like the one hidden inside Saturn’s moon Enceladus? This question has sparked a host of interesting studies that have mostly come to the same conclusion: maybe! In the newest addition to this tradition, scientists analyzed how the chemical composition of the moon’s core might impact its habitability. The team modelled the production of life-essential elements collectively known as CHNOPS—carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulfur—with three simulated compositions: primordial, composite or slightly modified, and non-primordial.While we already that Enceladus contains the complete sextet, the study suggests that primordial or composite cores are able “to justify the production of all the essential CHNOPS elements,” according to the study.“Due to the growing evidence of a global water ocean with large biological potential in its interior, the Saturn moon Enceladus has been subject to continuous studies,” said researchers led by Alberto Flandes of the National Autonomous University of Mexico. The team found that “a primordial core composition would favour the production of methane in considerably larger concentrations, while a composite core would favour the production of sulphate ions and hydrogen sulfide in larger concentrations.”To trot out one of my , all I want for Christmas is a life-seeking mission to Enceladus.Thanks for reading! See you next week.

item.title: Google Will Soon Share Android Developers' Addresses Publicly
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
"Starting on March 1, 2027, Google will display Android developers' phone numbers and addresses with their apps," reports Engadget, "and users everywhere will be able to see them."
As The Elec has reported, this decision has been met with criticism, specifically from smaller developers who operate out of their homes... [Google] says they have to classify themselves as a trader if they intend to earn money from their apps in any way on a regular basis, and if they already have a consistent frequency of transactions... Once they classify themselves as a trader, they'll have to submit their business identity, phone number and address, which Google will display to users everywhere...
If they fail to comply with these requirements, Google could block their updates from rolling out. Ultimately, the company could remove their apps from the Play store, not just in Europe, but in all regions around the world. The Verge notes that Google doesn't accept PO Boxes for an address like Apple does, forcing people to think of ways to protect their identifying information while still earning money from their apps.
Google said it takes privacy seriously, but with a spokesperson telling Engadget that in addition "we comply with applicable laws" and that Google recognizes "how important it is for users to have accessible support for the apps they install.
"Based on what we have heard from the developer community, we are exploring ways to minimize the developer information displayed publicly while making sure users can still easily reach developers for support."

item.title: GTA VI: Console Shortages, Performance Showdowns, $1B More Sales, and Some Tech Issues
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Grand Theft Auto VI "has caused a worldwide shortage of gaming consoles," reports the Washington Post, with the game only playable on the most recent generation of Microsoft's Xbox (Series X or S) or on PlayStation 5: In the United States, Sony's higher-end PlayStation 5 Pro was intermittently sold out even before the release, with major retailers out of stock at its $900 retail price and resellers asking as much as $1,900. In Germany, stores such as MediaMarkt and Saturn are sold out of PS5 models and lower-end Xbox ones... Consoles at Sony-recommended prices are similarly hard to find in other European countries, with third-party resellers offering the device at nearly double the price. In Japan, Sony has gone as far as restricting who is allowed to buy the console to block scalpers. The Sony Store sells it only through a lottery open to buyers with a Japanese account and at least 60 hours of verified PS4 or PS5 playtime. Windows Central notes Xbox One consoles can also stream GTA 6 from Xbox Cloud Gaming. And they argue that Sony's "Plays best on PS5" tagline for GTA 6 "is a lie, it turns out," citing a comparison from the hardware-reviewing YouTube channel Digital Foundry (which has 1.54 million subscribers):
Digital Foundry's analysis seems to suggest in no uncertain terms that the Xbox Series X version is generally superior to the PS5. Digital Foundry says that the PS5 version suffers from frame rate issues far more frequently than the Xbox Series X... The Xbox Series X version supports VRR, which with a compatible display helps offset frame drops and smooth out performance perception. GTA 6's sandbox is among the most complex in history, so it's an impressive feat that it runs as well as it does in general on both PS5 and Xbox Series X systems... This is without Xbox Series X leveraging FSR 4.1 either, which in theory, could push the visuals on Xbox Series X beyond even that of the extremely expensive PS5 Pro. In the end they also acknowledge that "the differences are negligible in reality." But the site TechPowerUp notes recent estimates by Alinea Analytics that PlayStation 5 accounts for 75.7% share of GTA VI sales, or 40 million sales, vs. just 13 million units on Xbox. That's 53 million sales total, representing "an estimated total revenue figure of $4.7 billion... "[P]layer statistics show that around 250,000 players have already spent over 100 hours in-game in its first week."
Meanwhile, The Times of India reports both PS5 and Xbox owners are experiencing console issues that may be related to overheating:
A Polish console repair technician says his workshop has seen a sharp rise in faulty Xbox consoles since GTA 6 came out earlier this month. Xbox is far less common than PlayStation in Poland. Even so, it now accounts for around two of every 10 consoles the shop receives each day. Before GTA 6 came out, it took in roughly 10 Xbox units a month.Owners report overheating, shutdowns mid-session, boot failures and slowdowns. Some machines refuse to install updates or freeze after one. One Series X ran other titles fine but stopped booting after a few days of GTA 6. It now powers on with no video output, then the fan stops and the machine shuts itself off. No common cause has been found yet. Overheating is the main suspect, but Xbox diagnostic tools are limited, so the shop is building its own to read error codes.
PS5 owners ran into trouble first. One unit that kept switching off mid-session logged 40 Main SoC Access Errors, plus seven APU VRM Power Fail and seven SSD Controller Watchdog errors. The technician says liquid metal shifting between the chip and heatsink, a known weak spot on older PS5 models, is often to blame...
A Twitch streamer's PS5 died mid-broadcast while he was riding an ATV through Leonida. The screen froze, artifacts appeared, and the system never booted again, even though there was little dust inside. Reddit posts tell similar stories. One Series X owner says the console would not power on the morning after a long session, and a dead power supply is suspected. Another managed about 10 minutes of play before a local repair shop blamed the motherboard...
Neither Microsoft nor Sony has confirmed that GTA 6 is behind the failures.
In related news, the social media team at Microsoft-owned GitHub "published and subsequently deleted a bizarrely brazen post on X," reports Kotaku. The tweet pointed to the 58,000 stars earned by a new project launched in August — the PlayStation5 emulator AnyPS5, which it said can be used for "rewriting PS5 executables to run on Windows and Linux. Does changing where games run cross a legal line?" [T]he video that was contained within GitHub's post highlighted that users' efforts to improve the AnyPS5 emulator were primarily driven by the release of GTA 6.
The article notes GTA VI's publisher Take Two has been "actively shooting down all of the GitHub repositories attempting to vibe-code a PC port of GTA 6 over the past week."

item.title: Will AI Bots Ever Catch on for Online Shopping?
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
"If you currently use an AI agent that signs in to your account with your credentials, it may no longer be able to connect," American Express told its customers today (according to Slashdot reader Smonster). And ahile Walmart's site welcomes AI agents, there's blocks or limitations on them from Amazon, eBay, Kohl's and United Airlines, CNBC reports. And other sites "have added provisions to their terms of service spelling out that they're not liable if users' AI-driven purchases go wrong..."
The hiccups threaten to stunt the growth of shopping agents by creating a clunky and frustrating experience for users who are just starting to experiment with the tools. The question of who takes the blame when a transaction goes wrong also remains unclear.
Despite those challenges, analysts remain bullish about agentic commerce's potential. U.S. revenue from agentic commerce could reach up to $1 trillion by 2030, analysts at McKinsey and ICSC forecast in April. Retailers and tech companies are also positioning agents as a helping hand for holiday shopping. Walmart on Tuesday touted its partnership with Meta, saying consumers could "put an AI agent to work" to nab Black Friday deals....
For users hoping to turn their online shopping over to AI agents, the experience can be unpredictable. Agents encounter a patchwork of permissions across various websites. Retailers such as Coach and Gap allow AI bots to browse but not check out, while others such as Target sometimes "block shopping agents by accident," according to an audit conducted in August by agent security company Billions Network. Amazon has responded the most aggressively to agents by walling off its site entirely. The company rankled Elon Musk last month after it prevented his Grok Bot from placing orders. In September, the company also blocked Meta's Muse from shopping on its platform, saying it never agreed to participate in the program. And last November, Amazon sued Perplexity, accusing the startup of concealing its Comet agent, which can purchase products on behalf of users. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said the company expects "over time, to partner with third-party agents," but that any partnerships will require the right "value exchange" between agents and retailers... For now, agents remain a niche tool for shopping, with agentic purchases making up just 0.4% of global e-commerce transactions and 0.2% of value, according to Bain & Co. research published earlier this month... But retailers may not be able to ignore them forever. Roughly a quarter of Muse's 10 million users are shopping online via an AI agent with an average spend of $200 per order, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said in October. The article notes bots often "get stumped by login requirements at checkout. In some cases, the agents may require human intervention to bypass a Captcha test and continue browsing...
"A Visa study published earlier this month instructed 22 models from 12 AI labs to carry out a range of shopping tasks, such as buying a TV, a laptop and a hair appliance. The agents failed about 43% of test runs, and in more than half of those failed runs, an agent purchased a product "that did not meet the customer's identified requirements," according to the study..."

item.title: Chinese Data Center Tied to Alice Huang Found Using Nvidia's Powerful AI Chips
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Friday Nvidia's stock showed a 30.95% drop over the last month, and a 37% drop from its October 2nd high of $239.24. But it managed a 4.83% gain for the week — after some bad news hit Friday morning...
A Chinese data center with ties to Alice Huang (the suspected Chinese spy-agency asset) "has installed hardware with Nvidia's powerful Blackwell AI chips," writes Gizmodo, citing a Friday morning report from Bloomberg. Those chips are "among Nvidia's most powerful products," writes Bloomberg, and their presence was confirmed by "a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November," (offering the hardware as collateral for a $14 million loan, according to bank filings seen by Bloomberg News). A second Chinese company (this one controlled by a Tokyo-based parent company) also described a server with Nvidia's advanced Blackwell chips in documents for a similar loan in late 2025 from, Bloomberg reports:
The submissions reveal for the first time that Nvidia's Blackwell processors found their way into a Chinese data center that has ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. [Alice Huang has ties to "a number of companies" that invested in the second company, and its president is her husband Kang Wei.]
These processors were until recently Nvidia's most powerful data center products, and they've always been illegal to ship to China without a US license. President Donald Trump has explicitly said he doesn't want these chips — which OpenAI and Anthropic PBC use to train their most cutting-edge models — going to the Asian country, at least for now. Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, meanwhile, once claimed they were too big to smuggle: a standard two-meter-tall GB300 NVL72 server rack, which contains 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, can weigh more than 1,500 kilograms (3,300 pounds) and is about the size of a gigantic fridge...
Shanghai Shuoyao — the company that procured the GB300 rack and offered it as collateral — is active at the data center linked to Alice Huang and also has significant overlap with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is under US investigation over concerns that it smuggled Nvidia chips to China, Bloomberg has reported. Shanghai Shuoyao, which hasn't responded to Bloomberg queries over the past year, confirmed this month in a rare public statement that it is one of Megaspeed's service providers, describing the partnership as "limited to ordinary commercial cooperation."
Megaspeed, meanwhile, used a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project in 2024 to describe its largest data center to investors, dubbing the site a "specific area" facility in an unnamed country... The parameters they've outlined in construction plans reviewed by Bloomberg — specifically, the total processing power as compared to the energy input — would be extremely difficult to satisfy with chips from Chinese companies such as Huawei Technologies Co.
Bloomberg says Nvidia "has not answered repeated queries," though they add that Nvida "for years insisted that there was no black market for its products."
The article also notes that Megaspeed (where Alice Huang worked) "won a coveted stamp of approval from Nvidia within four days of its creation" in 2023, and went on to become Nvidia's largest customer in Southeast Asia.

item.title: Mozilla Thanks Users For New Features in Firefox 161: Site-Specific VPN and Keyboard Shortcuts
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Firefox 161 (released Tuesday) promises "A better Firefox, thanks to you. All of these improvements began with a community request." In a Thanksgiving-themed message, they wrote "Here's to the passionate people who keep us moving forward."
Choose which sites always open with VPN. Our free built-in VPN just got one of its most requested upgrades. Pick sites where the VPN always turns on, and sites where it stays off because they work better without it. Bonus: VPN data is unlimited through January. Use it as much as you like until then... Set your own shortcuts . Create keyboard shortcuts for what you use most, like opening tabs, saving pages or closing windows. Type "about:keyboard" in the address bar.
See images appear as they load. Firefox now supports JPEG XL, an image format that lets you see a preview of the full image before it downloads.
Neowin notes Firefox is also committing to its redesign:
Mozilla has been trying to win over users from Chromium-based browsers, hoping they pick up Firefox. To do so, aside from still supporting uBlock Origin, the firm made a big design shift this year by introducing Nova, so that users on the other side can feel they are familiar with it, as it brings the more common, modern rounded corner design philosophy, which Google's Chrome has been using for quite a while... However, as is usually the case, not everyone has been on-board with Nova and they are completely fine to feel that way; Mozilla also understands this which is why it offered a way to opt-out of it by tweaking a configuration setting via about:config. However, this week the firm announced that it is going to take that option away.
In a post on its official Mozilla Connect forum, which was shared with us by Neowin forum member ecmram, the Firefox team confirmed that it will remove the config toggle preference for reverting to the old design next month in December. The company says that the rollout of Nova is now complete, and it wants to lock the preference to ensure that Firefox performs as intended and to prevent unexpected browser behavior. As such, anyone who has previously used the browser.nova.enabled preference to disable the redesign will automatically get Nova starting next month, thus wiping the official way to return to the previous UI once the change takes effect.
On the positive side, Mozilla is not entirely ignoring feedback from users who are unhappy with the redesign. The company says it has introduced several changes based on community feedback, including a new set of Classic Themes with the latest version 161, that offer flat colors without gradients. These can be found under about:addons, and one of them even mimics the older Proton design with a gray appearance. There is a new Fire toolbar button too that clears history with a single-click.

item.title: Nvidia Seeded Pirated Books and Shared Them With Adobe, Authors Allege
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TorrentFreak: Several book authors have filed (PDF) an amended complaint accusing Nvidia of seeding pirated books via BitTorrent, after downloading them from shadow libraries including Anna's Archive and LibGen. [...] These tools can download files via BitTorrent, and the authors and Nvidia both agree that whether they also upload data to others depends on the settings used. According to the authors, Nvidia didn't prevent seeding altogether. "When Nvidia ran the BitTorrent client, Nvidia uploaded pieces of pirated book files to third parties during the downloading process (i.e., before the download was complete). Nvidia also 'seeded' pirated books (i.e., made available and uploaded parts of a completely downloaded file). While Nvidia took some steps to limit seeding, it did not prevent seeding altogether," the complaint reads.
The authors say they found out in June, when Nvidia handed over the code it used for torrenting. Based on that code, they were "able to determine that Nvidia did not disable uploading," the authors told the court. The complaint states that the authors' own books were among those Nvidia downloaded. However, the claim that they were also uploaded to others is made "on information and belief," which essentially means the authors don't have direct knowledge of it. In addition to the seeding claims, the authors also allege that Nvidia shared the pirated books with business partners, including Adobe, through a "PDF Extraction Project" involving 250 million pages. These pages were acquired in part from shadow libraries such as Anna's Archive and LibGen.
According to the complaint, Nvidia shared its pirated books with Adobe because it wanted to "get tokens out of PDFs to create differentiated models" and "include PDF extraction into our NeMo pipeline so that customers can leverage their PDF content." In return, the complaint says, Adobe committed to using Nvidia's language models in some of its products. That made the deal a big opportunity for Nvidia, with its NeMo AI models potentially "powering every one of Adobe PDFs," the authors write. Adobe wasn't the only partner. The complaint also mentions partnerships with Cohere and Imbue that involved sharing Nvidia's base training data and offering books acquired from shadow libraries. The authors believe their own books were shared with all three companies, but this is alleged on information and belief. With these allegations, the amended complaint now accuses Nvidia of distributing the books itself and of helping others to infringe, which falls under its existing direct and contributory infringement claims.

item.title: James T. Russell, Physicist Who Pioneered CD and DVD Technology, Dies At 95
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
James T. Russell, the American physicist whose pioneering digital-to-optical recording and playback system laid the foundation for CD, DVD and Blu-ray technology, has died at the age of 95. "Russell never became a household name, but the technology he developed, later licensed by Sony and Phillips, would transform everything from the way people listen to music to the way data is stored," reports The Daily Chronicle. From the report: In a career spanning almost his entire life, Russell earned more than 70 patents, but his biggest breakthrough was the invention of the first digital-to-optical recording and playback system in the 1960s and early 1970s, a system that brought crystal clear audio and film to the masses. [...] It was in Richland that Russell started exploring how to create cleaner recordings of music. Popping and hissing often accompanied the music of vinyl records, from the analog sound of a needle scraping against microgrooves, and Russell thought he could do something about it. He crunched the numbers before bringing an invention report to Battelle: What if a light beam could read a digital record?
"It isn't clear what the problem was," Russell recalled in a Seattle Times interview in 2004. "I think there was some feeling amongst the moneybags that it probably wouldn't work, (or) if it did work there's no advantage, no value in optical records. What would you use it for, and would people want it and, anyway, if it was any good, IBM would have already invented it." While his idea faced skepticism early on, the company gave him some money to experiment. Russell invented an early method to store audio digitally and play it back to produce a flawless sound. He also created a way to store digital information densely.
Other primitive, analog laser disk technology had been developed in the 1950s by engineer David Paul Gregg. Russell's earliest patents in the field were issued in the mid-1960s, with a working prototype finished by the 1970s, using a laser to read binary data on a compact disc, or CD. The patent for Russell's invention passed from company to company, bringing him from Richland to Salt Lake City, then to Toronto. His development of the first digital-to-optical recording and playback system became foundational to CD-ROM, DVD and Blu-ray technology. Russell didn't earn royalties, never made a fortune, and was rarely credited for his work.

item.title: Scientists Used Seabirds To Track Hidden Ships
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Scientists equipped seabirds with audio recorders and GPS trackers to detect fishing vessels that were not broadcasting their locations through the Automatic Identification System (AIS), according to a new study published in Science Advances. They found that unseen vessels accounted for about 32% of vessel-related audio detections in the North Atlantic and 12% in the Mediterranean. "The one petrel in the study interacted with vessels in the South Pacific, but its geolocation device was damaged, so it was not possible to calculate how many ships it encountered had their trackers off," adds 404 Media. From the report: Many vessels are required to continuously signal their location using the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which openly broadcasts a ship's location, similar to flight tracking. But AIS can be disabled for legitimate reasons -- such as evading pirates -- or with more nefarious motivations, such as concealment of illegal fishing activities. The new study was not designed to interrogate why any particular vessel switched off its AIS tracker. However, the discovery that seabirds are regularly interacting with unseen ships can shed light on broader efforts to monitor commercial fisheries, while also revealing new insights about seabird behavior, especially their risk of becoming "bycatch" when they are fatally trapped in fishing gear.
Unseen vessel activity "is concerning, or at least important, regardless of whether it's legal or illegal," said Jonathan Rutter, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Oxford who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. He added that the recordings were not intended to be used for law-enforcement or surveillance, but that this line of research could become a "powerful tool for improving risk assessment" by recording seabird-vessel interactions that would otherwise be off the map.

Denver prosecutors declined to file criminal charges, deeming the case a civil matter, but are continuing to collect evidence and explore legal options to stop the behavior. The driver remains unidentified.

item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
The New York Times is instructing freelance photographers not to use Adobe Photoshop 2027 (version 28.0.0 and subsequent updates), warning that its new AI features operate "in ways that may not be apparent to users" and "can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated." The Verge reports: It's not always clear which tools in Adobe's apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers' trust.
Last year, the Times said that it does not "retouch or digitally manipulate" photos but may "make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image." In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos.

item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Australia's Parliament has passed the Digital Duty of Care Act, requiring online platforms to proactively identify and mitigate foreseeable harms or face potentially billions of dollars in fines. The Record reports: Platforms are required to detect and decrease risks from harmful content and must bolster protections for users under 18 against pornography, suicide and eating disorders. They also must undertake annual written risk assessments and call out major platform design changes such as endless scrolling that create new harms. Under the law, users also will be able to opt out of algorithmic feeds and will be required to prove their age to access porn.
[...] U.S. officials have accused the Australian legislation of violating free speech, threatening American companies' business models and imposing vague requirements that will cause tech giants to overhaul their services to avoid liability. "We are particularly concerned by potential mandates that would allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements -- such as forced chronological feeds or opt-in recommendation systems," the U.S. Embassies and Consulates in Australia said in a September public comment. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told Parliament in October that "rather than someone in the United States deciding" what people see, now Australians can "decide themselves." The law will require platforms to "give us more choice over the content and the features that we use, including the feeds that we choose," he said.
"This is a victory for our children and young people. The dangers were unforeseen when the digital world was young. But now that the digital world has matured, they can be easily recognized and they can be remedied."

item.title: Anthropic Created a Honeypot To Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren, a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures. The test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sits just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that's cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps.
[...] Earlier versions of Claude are much more likely to fall into the honeypot trap than newer models, according to test runs with Siren. The more recent models have been given additional training designed to make them less likely to break the rules when performing agentic tasks. "We've added this in both our supervised learning sets and a few reinforcement learning environments," says Oscar O'Rahilly, an Anthropic researcher who specializes in AI training and who helped develop Siren. "This could be a driving factor for why it has improved so much." O'Rahilly says that models reason about whether to give in to temptation, which may partly explain why smarter models are less likely to break bad. Siren experiments also showed that giving Claude a simple additional piece of text explaining that it should not escape the sandbox resulted in drastically fewer efforts to break free.
In Anthropic's tests, Claude 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.2 fell for the honeypot between 0.6 and 1.6 percent of the time. Two earlier models, Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5, went rogue 12.7 percent and 25.8 percent of the time, respectively. AI models are sometimes known to behave better if they know they're being tested. But O'Rahilly says other experiments suggest that Claude actually behaves more responsibly if it thinks a scenario is real rather than a test. As AI models get ever smarter, many researchers worry about whether they'll outwit their human counterparts. If that does happen, then it may be essential that agents -- and not just the executives responsible for them -- can resist temptation.

item.title: All the Worst Government GTA Memes from Around the World
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: is a true . Every news channel is covering it, anyone with a passing interest in video games is playing it, and it’s in less than a week. Desperate to connect with constituents, governments around the world have tried to capitalize on GTA’s popularity by releasing some of the worst AI-generated memes I’ve ever seen. The pictures of politicians in the hyper-real cartoon pink-tinted style of GTA 6 are so awful they even caused a minor political scandal in Scotland.Let’s begin in the United States, where Vice President JD Vance, the White House, and several other government-run X accounts attempted to capture the cultural zeitgeist by quickly churning out AI-generated meme garbage. GTA has long been popular with Trump 2.0 officials. In March, the official X account of the White House published a compilation of strikes on Iranian targets overlaid with the “WASTED” game over screen from GTA. In one of the more embarrassing exchanges, the X account for House Republicans posted an AI-generated picture of Hakeem Jefferies, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Abdul El-Sayed above the words “Grand Theft Taxpayer.” A Democrat-linked account then replied with its own picture of Trump and the words “Grand Theft Autocrat.” Embarrassing for all involved.Israel also got in on the action. On the Friday after the game’s release, U.S. ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee shared a “Shabbot Shalom” meme in the GTA style. The Israel Defense Force’s Farsi X account posted several pictures of dead Iranian officials captioned as “WASTED.”“We saw all this killing before GTA6,” the post said in Persian, referring to the now retired meme we got something before GTA 6. This account posts in Farsi and meant for “direct dialogue between us and you,” meaning Israel and Iran, according to its bio on X.In India, Prime Minister Narenda Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) posted GTA memes repeatedly on November 19, the day the game was released.Indian politician and frequent Modi critic Jairam Ramesh mocked Modi for the posts on social media. “The PM in a desperate bid to reach out to the youth has resorted to GTA V and GTA VI imagery on social media,” Ramesh . “Recall that this video game follows a criminal duo. How very appropriate.”On Instagram, Singapore’s Land Transport Authority made fun of people who can’t navigate the country’s rail system. “If he can memorize the entire GTA6 map, he can memorize the Singapore MRT System Map,” . “Bro knows every corner of Leonida but still saves the SG MRT System Map on his phone to get to Orchard. 💀”NATO posted its attempt at being part of the cultural conversation on Instagram. “Wanted level: NATO,” the post said above the pink-hued cross cut collage of military images in the GTA style. “The final boss of wanted levels. Think you could fend off the most successful Alliance in history? NATO isn’t part of GTA6 of course, but if it was, we think even the best gamers would have a challenge with this one.”In Scotland, the Scottish National Party (SNP) posted GTA 6 memes so cringe that they talked about it on the floor of parliament. On November 19, the SNP social media accounts posted AI-generated pictures of Boris Johnson and Margaret Thatcher in the GTA style. “When the loading screen so long you start seeing characters you’ve never seen before,” one image said over a picture of Thatcher pouring a bag of “Scottish oil money” into the UK treasury.Scotland’s Green Party didn’t find the memes funny. Rockstar is originally Scottish, was founded in Edinburgh, and still maintains a significant studio there. In parliament, Green co-leader Gillian Mackay said she was proud of what all of Rockstar’s workers had done to stand up against bad working conditions and produce a work of art like GTA 6. Then she made comments about SNP leader and Scottish First Minister John Swiney. “Last night the SNP angered anti-AI campaigners by posting AI-generated GTA memes on its social media despite huge concerns about the impact of AI and AI data centers on artists, workers, and the environment,” Mackay said in the parliament . “Does the first minister understand why people are concerned about his government’s approach to AI and the big companies behind it.”The SNP deleted the memes and Swiney apologized. “First of all, let me say that I don’t want to offend anyone by anything that we get up to, so if I’ve offended anyone about that, I’m sorry about that. It was not my intention,” Swiney said in the Scottish parliament. Then he said he shared concerns about AI but defended the technology’s use for healthcare.There will be more bad posts like this. hasn’t been out for even a week and the memetic landscape around it will shift and change. We don’t even know what the dominant memes for the game are yet, let alone the innovative ways posters will iterate on them. Rest assured, however, that the governments of the world are watching and waiting to post their own variations and make it all cringe.

item.title: Pass the Controller: How Single Console Households Split 'GTA VI'
item.author: Megan Farokhmanesh
item.content:encoded: is 2026’s breakout entertainment event. By the numbers, it made roughly $3.79 billion in revenue at launch, outpacing the lifetime earnings for megahit films like , , and . PlayStation called it their biggest launch of all time with over 39 million players on the platform alone. It’s the center of the current cultural zeitgeist, whether it’s because of the game’s , , , , or its .Entire households are playing GTA VI with one slight hitch: unlike movies, TV shows, or even books you can read side by side, a single-player, 40+ hour experience is tough to enjoy when you live together. For some couples, the solution has been using more than one console or even multiple copies of the game. Married couple Meagan Kelley and Kyle Prahl typically switch between playing different games in the same room, or the same platforms in different parts of the house. The two are parents who find time to game after putting their son to bed. “The nice thing about having really young kids is they do go to bed super early,” Kelley told me. “Usually [my son] goes down and is asleep before eight, so then that's kind of like our prime gaming time.” The couple often plays different games in the same room, but for GTA VI “we're playing separately, so that kind of sucks because it's like we don't get a lot of time for each other,” Kelley said. Although some men online have whined about central romance, complaining about doing favors for their in-game girlfriend Lucia (“cuck simulator” being one common refrain), Kelley says the benefits to her real-life relationship are only positive. “It's funny that there's so much online discourse about GTA splitting up relationships and stuff when it's like something that can bring Kyle and I closer,” Kelley said. “Especially as we become parents and need to have more perspective on making sure that we're making time for ourselves.” Dividing up time to play and sharing their experiences, she said, adds a new dimension to their mutual hobby. “When we are together taking care of our kid or having conversations, it's almost like book club,” Kelley said. “We share the different ways that we're experiencing the game with choices and stuff like that.” Justin Massongill, another GTA VI player, and his wife recently had their second child. “She's taken on a lot,” he said. He bought the game for her, giving her priority to play so she could de-stress.Massongill watched his wife play the first hour of the game; the next morning, he started his own. “We're kind of trying not to look too much at the other player's screen,” he said. “I don't want to, you know, get spoiled on things. But it's also such a massive game that what are the chances that we're going to see the same thing in the first place?”Madeline Blondeau and her fiancée decided to buy their copy of together. The $80 price tag wasn’t so bad between the two of them; they downloaded the game, knowing that even with a PlayStation 5 and a PlayStation 5 Pro, they’d have to divvy up time between their single copy. “We have been alternating our schedules,” Blondeau said. Her fiancée wakes up at 5 a.m. to start her IT job. Blondeau’s shift starts around 10 a.m. “We've sort of worked this out—me playing while she is working, and then her playing while I am finishing up my shift, trying to tiptoe around spoilers.” Even as a queer couple, there’s an equality and care for each other in the experience Blondeau finds reassuring. “I think there's these very gendered expectations in relationships in terms of who games, who is the gamer of the household,” Blondeau said. You even see it in , she adds, where Jason, the game’s male protagonist, will be the one with a controller in his hand. “Breaking down the gendered expectations of who is the gamer in the relationship really opens up a whole avenue for not getting into fights with your partner over video games,” Blondeau said. “It feels like two people who figure their shit out, working out equitable time to experience something they've liked their whole lives, and talk about it.”This past weekend, Blondeau’s fiancé left to grab groceries. She came back with something extra: the trilogy for Nintendo Switch, a consolation prize for whoever wasn’t playing their shared copy of GTA VI. “I was in the mood to play Vice City,” her partner said. “We can trade off."

item.title: Physicists Send an Unblockable Message Using Gravity
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Longtime Slashdot reader fahrbot-bot shares a report from Phys.org: University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter. The unusual experiment took place in UQ's Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between two levels, moving its 1.8 metric ton (4,000 pound) counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1. A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field and translated the message into a single word, "Gravity." The research has been published in Science Advances.
"Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path," [said Dr. Charles Woffinden from the School of Mathematics and Physics]. "While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block." Professor Andrew White said the biggest limitation to future gravity-based communication was its slow speed. "Our elevator was snail-paced -- it's from the 1950s -- so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word," White said.
"The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it and the sensitivity of the detector. Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modeling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 meters (1,640 feet) and data rates of around 15 bits per minute."

item.title: GTA 6 Streams Hit With Takedowns Over In-Game Reggaeton Song
item.author: Timothy Geigner
item.content:encoded: Unless you’re a monk on retreat somewhere, you know that was released in recent days and that roughly the entire world is playing it. And, importantly, putting clips of the game online, or featuring it in let’s play game streams. I haven’t played this thing yet, but I am enjoying the clips. My personal favorites are the ones where the player goes around and randomly throws a basketball at people’s faces. Gets me right in the id.Now, Rockstar Games has not been shy about DMCAing the shit out of anything it doesn’t like when it comes to its games. The company tries to DMCA leaks out of existence, which never works. It’s also happy to takedown mods for previewing future game content in them and the like. But a recent spate of stream takedowns apparently had nothing to do with Rockstar and might have been YouTube’s Content ID automatic system. On Nov. 22, streamers who uploaded their GTA 6 gameplay on YouTube were suddenly hit with a barrage of copyright strikes. They all came from a single source: Colombian reggaeton artist Frank “El Santo.” The Medellín-born singer and songwriter, whose real name is Andrés Mauricio Arango Flórez, played GTA 6 on stream on his YouTube channel. His footage was then used to auto-claim copyright on anyone who was playing the game live on YouTube. This resulted in indiscriminate strikes against users, including big channels such as theRadBrad (14.1 million subscribers) and HollowPoiint (5.2 million subscribers).This seemingly absurd situation arose from a combination of specific circumstances and YouTube’s often-criticized copyright policies. Frank El Santo’s YouTube channel contains his official music videos, so it’s possible that the platform mistakenly deemed the GTA 6 gameplay video eligible for copyright claims. After commenters pointed out the issue during his stream, Arango Flórez deleted the gameplay video, but the copyright strikes continued until the YouTube team intervened.Now, there’s been some speculation out in the wild that Arango Florez might still have taken some action that resulted in Content ID going kazoo with the takedowns. He insists otherwise. Ultimately, it doesn’t matter all that much, because the real point here is that YouTube’s takedown system remains so absolutely wide open to error, fraud, and abuse that content that pretty much nobody thinks should be taken down gets taken down anyway across a wide swath of targets.Regardless of the intent, this episode highlights that YouTube’s copyright policies are either ineffective or outright damaging to its users. The company relies on automated processes and AI-assisted tools to detect copyright infringement​​​​​​​, often resulting in videos being taken down or demonetized without proper reason. As HollowPoiint put it in a post on X where he praised YouTube’s quick intervention to resolve the GTA 6 El Santo issue, “Now we just need a better system in place.”This isn’t a revelation. We’ve been saying this . YouTube’s automatic system has been responsible for a legion of bad takedowns, some of them so absurd it boggles the mind. In the exact moment when Rockstar should, and probably does, want as much of this user hype content out there as possible, some combination of this artist and YouTube got a bunch of streams taken down.It’s well past time this was fixed. YouTube… what are you waiting for?

item.title: World Has Six Consecutive Days 2C Above Preindustrial Levels For First Time
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from The Guardian: For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned. This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating. The daily global surface temperature rose to its highest ever point above preindustrial levels, 2.24C, on Monday, the most recent day for which data is available, and is forecast to persist at similarly high levels for at least several more days. "This will amplify the buildup of CO2 in the atmosphere driven by fossil fuel burning," said Richard Betts, the head of climate impacts research at the Met Office Hadley Centre. "The CO2 increase from this year to next will be about 3.5 parts per million, a third faster than in recent years and nearly twice as fast as what it should have been limited to if we'd been on track to limit global warming to 1.5C."
Zeke Hausfather, a climate researcher at Berkeley Earth, said: "Another day, another global temperature record," adding that the previous record of 2.05C over the 1850-1900 baseline, set in 2023, has been "smashed."

item.title: Suspected Chinese Agents Are Trying to Dupe Americans with Fake Listings on Job Platforms
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
"LinkedIn is probably the greatest intelligence tool that's ever been created," CNN heard from Holden Triplett, director of counterintelligence at the National Security Council in the first Trump administration.
A LinkedIn spokesperson responded that "Creating a fake account or misrepresenting your identity is a clear violation of our terms of service." (And they also told CNN that LinkedIn remains "focused on detecting state-sponsored abuse and will continue to enforce our policies against fake accounts.") But it's not just happening on LinkedIn...
Suspected Chinese spies have created an elaborate web of fake firms with job opportunities aimed at tricking current and former US officials into divulging government secrets as part of a scheme that is more pervasive than previously reported, CNN has found. Interviews with a dozen people caught up in the operation — as well as CNN analysis of suspected bogus websites — reveal how there is a much broader target pool for obtaining sensitive US information after the Trump administration laid off thousands of federal employees. [CNN reported in 2025 that "foreign powers such as China and Russia" had directed their intelligence services "to ramp up recruiting of Americans working in national security by targeting those who had been fired or felt they were at risk of losing their jobs".] These workers left their posts with inadequate guidance and protection from spying plots, ex-officials said, creating a potentially valuable resource for Beijing and weak spot for Washington... In addition to government workers, the plot has targeted journalists, trade consultants and others, who might have knowledge deemed valuable to US adversaries.
The FBI offered a glimpse into the malicious recruiting scam when it seized 13 websites officials say were tied to fake consulting firms in June. China denied the FBI allegations. CNN analyzed the sites' software code, looked at other suspicious job listings, and interviewed people approached by similar companies. CNN identified several more websites that mimicked the style and substance of those disabled by the FBI. Two more sites that Max Lesser, a senior analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank, discovered and shared with CNN have some of the same web infrastructure or other connections to the seized websites. In total, Lesser has uncovered more than 100 other web domains, many of which share similar characteristics with the sites taken down by the FBI....
This sprawling network has the hallmarks of a Chinese intelligence operation, Lesser told CNN.
After creating fake web sites, the operatives "plant vague, well-paying job ads for consulting positions focused on China-related issues" on jobs sites like LinkedIn, CNN reports, asking applicants to produce "research reports". ("[D]ozens or hundreds of such reports, across various topics of interest to Beijing, can start to form a much clearer picture of US national security policy and its vulnerabilities, according to current and former FBI officials.")
CNN sent a detailed request for a comment to a spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington, DC. "I am not familiar with what you mentioned," they responded, adding that China "opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called 'Chinese spy' narrative."

item.title: DOJ Again Admits To Lying As Yet Another Trump Revenge Prosecution Starts To Fall Apart
item.author: Tim Cushing
item.content:encoded: The DOJ is nothing more than Trump’s revenge squad. Everyone Trump thinks has wronged him — whether it’s people who just weren’t loyal enough or people that engaged in investigations of his actions — is a target. That’s why Trump has pulled VP J.D. Vance from his peacekeeping mission in Iran to focus on “Democrat fraud.” That’s why the DOJ has been shedding talent since year one of Trump’s second term. And that’s why Trump has decided now is the time to see if he can’t turn Rep. Ilhan Omar into another one of his mass deportation victims. United States President Donald Trump has called for Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar to resign from the US Congress, reviving allegations of identity fraud after a court filing identified the Minnesota politician by an additional name.The DOJ filing, submitted on Wednesday, refers to Omar as “Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar” – “a/k/a” is an abbreviation for “also known as”.The document filed by the administration does not establish that Omar committed fraud.Oh, well. It didn’t stop a magistrate judge from approving a search warrant for Omar’s residence. And nothing seen so far indicates the federal court handling the (retaliatory) criminal case is ready to pull the plug on this bullshit. But if there’s anything that’s going to kill Trump’s case dead, it will be whatever remains of his DOJ legal representation which has routinely misled courts and, in other cases, baldly admitted it no longer has the personnel to capably handle everything Trump wants it do. A DOJ stretched to the breaking point by mass deportation activities simply doesn’t have the spare cycles to slip retaliatory prosecutions of Trump’s enemies past the courts. Once again, a federal court has caught the DOJ “misrepresenting” things in court, this time in relation to the ongoing investigation of Rep. Omar. “Caught” might be a bit too charitable to the court, since it was the admitting to malfeasance (but only after the court demanded more info from a DOJ that no longer has a healthy relationship with this part of the system of checks and balances). The Justice Department admitted Tuesday that it misrepresented the position of the House’s top lawyer in multiple filings seeking to justify its handling of the Oct. 12 raid of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington residence.Prosecutors told a magistrate judge that House General Counsel Matthew Berry “refused” to intervene in the search and instead endorsed the Trump administration’s view that searches of lawmakers’ private homes are not protected by the Constitution’s “speech or debate” clause, which shields lawmakers from prosecutorial scrutiny for their official conduct.The DOJ might have gotten away with this lie if it weren’t for those meddling kids. Well… one meddling kid, specifically: House General Counsel Matthew Berry. What the DOJ generously refers to as a “misrepresentation” is what everyone else would call a “lie.” Certainly the DOJ would call a misrepresentation a lie, especially if the misrepresentation occurred during a conversation with a federal officer.But it gave itself a pass in its filing, because of course it did. It called the seemingly deliberate misrepresentation of Berry’s legal advice an “inadvertent misunderstanding.” That might be believable if all that came from it was some minor procedural errors. But what’s being justified here under the “oh no our reading comprehension” is the search of a congressional rep’s residence for the sole purpose of trying to find literally anything at all that might justify an expulsion from Congress and/or the United States itself.In those filings, DOJ claimed Berry “refused to be involved,” and instead agreed with prosecutors’ view that lawmakers’ constitutional protections “do not extend to a Member’s private residence.”But the exchange between Berry and McCotter shows a much more limited response than prosecutors portrayed.Rather than embrace any limits on the “speech or debate” clause or its extension to private homes, Berry said House lawyers were not empowered to advocate for lawmakers who are the subject of criminal probes because their interests may diverge from the House’s. Had prosecutors searched a congressional office, Berry told McCotter, it would be more appropriate for his office to play a role. McCotter responded that evening: “Understood — Thanks for your time and consideration.” Twelve hours later, Department of Homeland Security agents arrived at Omar’s residence to carry out the search.The House counsel said it was only likely to be involved in very specific situations. Berry may have agreed the “speech and debate” clause that generally provides immunity to congressional reps for their statements would (obviously) not shield them from a search of their residence if some criminal act was suspected. But Berry definitely say he supported or approved of any raid of Ilhan Omar’s home.But the DOJ chose to say he did, hoping that paraphrasing an email from Berry would slid this past the magistrate judge and — beyond that — the judge handling the ensuing prosecution. But it didn’t work. And the moment others entered the fray to fight for the right to make Trump angry without being immediately subjected to a criminal investigation, the DOJ was forced to admit the stuff it said wasn’t honestly representative of the stuff it chose to misquote. And this seems like it’s going to result in another threat of sanctioning by yet another court.And that’s because the DOJ is so compromised it can’t stop doing exactly this sort of thing. If the DOJ actually cared about justice, it wouldn’t need to lie nearly as often as it does. But since it’s just a floppy Trump appendage, this is just going to keep happening until Trump finally leaves office.

item.title: Ohio’s Anti-SLAPP Law Works: Rep. Max Miller Loses Re-Election, Then His SLAPP Suit
item.author: Mike Masnick
item.content:encoded: Ohio Rep. Max Miller seems like a pretty bad person. Despite years of reporting about his history as being abusive to women, the story seemed to finally break through earlier this year when Mother Jones did an incredible deep dive into the evidence on Miller’s abusive behavior towards his ex-wife, Emily Moreno (the daughter of Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno) and their 2-year-old child. Some of the reporting was absolutely stunning:Records of the investigation into potential child abuse show that Moreno told detectives that Miller had previously thrown hot water at her, shoved her, and held a gun to her head; therefore, she couldn’t rule out that Miller caused their daughter’s fracture. Moreover, a child protection specialist reviewing the incident had characterized the bruising near the fracture as resembling a “handprint.”“Daddy’s house is scary,” Moreno recounted her daughter saying, according to a Bay Village, Ohio,relating to the February 2026 injury.The summary of the Zoom meeting andare among more than 2,000 pages of court filings and police reports pertaining to Miller that Mother Jones obtained through public records requests. The trove of documents contains allegations ofby Miller, misogyny and verbal abuse, and violent behavior against multiple women. The filings also includethat Miller implicitly threatened his ex-father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno.Some details had already come out a few months earlier, when the UK’s Daily Mail reported that Miller had been accused of “hurling a pot of boiling water” at Moreno, which already seemed pretty problematic. The further reporting from Mother Jones just served to further back up some of that original reporting.Soon after that Daily Mail article came out in May, Miller filed an extremely ill-conceived SLAPP suit against his ex-wife and her lawyers. He argued that the story was part of the custody battle over the ex-couple’s child. Then, in August, Miller did a livestream on X denying the allegations and pointed viewers to a Dropbox folder that he said would exonerate him, stuffed with sensitive information about his family and the divorce and custody fight. But it also, somewhat horrifically, included an unredacted nude photo of their two-year-old child. Miller’s lawyer, Aaron Minc, admitted that he fucked up in including a photo of the naked child in the documents. Apology or not, Moreno sued Miller and Minc on their daughter’s behalf over the horrifying incompetence of releasing such a sensitive photo to the world.Miller, who was up for re-election, kept insisting that this was all an attempt to harm his electability, and whether or not that was the case, he lost his re-election bid, fairly conclusively, getting 45.1% of the vote, compared to the winner, Brian Poindexter, who got 54.9%. That was a pretty big shift from two years earlier, when Miller defeated his then opponent by 15 points.Then, less than two weeks later, the judge in the SLAPP suit he filed against his ex-wife threw out the case, and is making Miller pay up for her legal fees (he’d already dropped her lawyers from the case), thanks to Ohio’s recently passed anti-SLAPP statute. The judge pointed out that Miller failed to establish a prima facie case for defamation (as required under the anti-SLAPP law’s burden shifting), in part because there’s a recording of him admitting that he had, in fact, poured hot water on her:An audio recording of the parties discussing the incident supports Defendant Moreno’s contention of truth. Defendant Moreno confronted Plaintiff about pouring “bowling [sic] hot water on me.” Although Plaintiff denies pouring hot water on her neck, he further admits the incident occurred. Plaintiff specifically stated “it was never done to hurt you with intent.” Plaintiff’s intent is irrelevant to the basic fact of whether the incident occurred, which addresses the element of falsity.Plaintiff maintains that the gist or sting of hurling a pot of boiling water is “categorically different” than the actions Plaintiff states actually occurred. It is Plaintiff’s burden to support his claims with credible, admissible evidence. Plaintiff has not shown that the statement about dousing Defendant Moreno with boiling hot water are false. The imputation that Plaintiff poured or doused Defendant Moreno with hot water is substantially true.Generally speaking, if there’s a recording of you admitting you did the thing you later sue someone for defamation over, it’s not going to go well for you.And, thanks to the new anti-SLAPP law (which is based on the increasingly common UPEPA anti-SLAPP statute from the Uniform Law Commission), the judge orders Miller to pay $76,762.38 in his ex-wife’s legal fees.So, in the course of less than two weeks, Miller lost his job and lost the bullshit vexatious lawsuit he filed against his ex-wife, for which he now needs to pay nearly $77k in her legal fees. Plus, the court found that the claim at the heart of his lawsuit, that he doused his ex-wife with hot water, is “substantially true.”And, of course, he’s still facing that lawsuit over revealing a nude photo of his toddler, though the same week he lost his re-election bid, he filed his own motion to dismiss, including an anti-SLAPP motion against the state-law claims. In it, he argues that the federal claim fails because publishing the naked photo of his child related to “a matter of public concern” which strikes me as somewhat outlandish. His reasoning is that the image documents the injury at the heart of the abuse allegations, meaning that releasing it falls under the statute’s exception for “matters of public concern.”Plaintiff now alleges that, even if the image was of public concern, the depicted anatomy was not, and that Defendants “could have redacted” it. But the exclusion turns on whether the action relates to a matter of public concern, not on whether each portion of an image was necessary to the speaker’s point. Plaintiff does not, and could not, allege that the disclosure of a document concerning the child’s injury, offered in response to public accusations about that injury, was unrelated to a matter of public concern.When you find yourself arguing whether the naked image of your injured child that you released to the internet is or is not a matter of public concern, I’d say you’ve already lost.

They found an overlooked router setting affected how it interfaced with other decades-old routers that the FAA is decommissioning, the source said. In the past, this kind of work typically involved at least six FAA employees. Under the Trump administration, it's now often coordinated by one employee: an FAA liaison. And there are only four people in the country with that title, according to sources familiar with the process.
The liaison's job involves coordinating and scheduling these upgrades — not approving them, sources said... The Trump administration's effort to move maintenance work along faster also eliminated a layer of FAA review that was critical to assessing risk [according to a source familiar with the process]. The union contends that process did not happen before L3Harris arrived at the El Dorado, Arkansas, site on November 13... item.title: The Birds Are Listening: Scientists Used Seabirds to Track Hidden Ships
item.author: Becky Ferreira
item.content:encoded: , our newsletter about the most exciting and mind-boggling science news and studies of the week. In what sounds like an avian riff on , scientists equipped seabirds with audio recorders in order to listen in on their interactions with fishing vessels across the world’s oceans, according to a study published on Wednesday in .The approach exposed a large number of so-called “unseen” vessels that did not have their location trackers switched on. Many vessels are required to continuously signal their location using the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which openly broadcasts a ship’s location, similar to flight tracking. But AIS can be disabled for legitimate reasons—such as evading pirates—or with more nefarious motivations, such as concealment of illegal fishing activities. The new study was not designed to interrogate why any particular vessel switched off its AIS tracker. However, the discovery that seabirds are regularly interacting with unseen ships can shed light on broader efforts to monitor commercial fisheries, while also revealing new insights about seabird behavior, especially their risk of becoming “bycatch” when they are fatally trapped in fishing gear.Unseen vessel activity “is concerning, or at least important, regardless of whether it's legal or illegal,” said Jonathan Rutter, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Oxford who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. He added that the recordings were not intended to be used for law-enforcement or surveillance, but that this line of research could become a “powerful tool for improving risk assessment” by recording seabird-vessel interactions that would otherwise be off the map. Rutter and his colleagues were inspired to combine these approaches by attaching audio recorders to three seabird species—the northern gannet, Balearic shearwater, and Westland petrel—which all frequently interact with fishing vessels. The team tracked the movements of the birds with GPS, and then analyzed whether the audio overlapped with AIS data at the same time and location during recorded interactions.The recordings showed that about 32 percent of the audio captured by seven gannets in the North Atlantic were from ships with their trackers off, while 12 percent of the audio captured by four shearwaters in the Mediterranean Sea were from unseen vessels. The one petrel in the study interacted with vessels in the South Pacific, but its geolocation device was damaged, so it was not possible to calculate how many ships it encountered had their trackers off.Rutter noted that the shearwaters were likely often interacting with smaller Mediterranean fishing boats that are not legally required to keep trackers on. However, the gannets encountered larger commercial vessels that are obligated to keep trackers active. While the researchers made a very conservative estimate that these birds visited unseen vessels for about one-third of the total duration of their daily encounters (or, about 22 minutes out of 68 minutes), it may well exceed half of that time.“The fact that we found at least one third, and probably more than one half, of the audio detections being unseen was pretty surprising,” Rutter said. “This is not the same thing as saying that half of vessels are unseen; it's half of the time that gannets go to vessels, those vessels are unseen.”“There are multiple reasons this could be,” he continued. “It could be illegal disabling, but at the same time, it could be poor satellite reception. There are lots of reasons that AIS can be off, and we want to emphasize that illegal fishing is a possibility, but that is not actually what we're showing. It's showing that there's a lot we're not seeing.”Seabirds are attracted to fishing vessels to feed on discarded catch, but many perish during these encounters after becoming tangled in lines or caught on baited hooks. Rutter and his colleagues hope that their study could help to prevent these deadly incidents, while also providing a new tool for monitoring unseen vessel activity. While this approach could enable real-time vessel detection, the team urged “caution in the use of animals as a fisheries surveillance tool, lest fishers come to mistrust scientists and/or marine animals themselves,” according to the study.Though environmental and commercial interests are often at odds, there is plenty of collaboration between fisheries and conservation scientists with the goal of sustainable and healthy long-term fish stock. Fisheries that adhere to regulations also have an interest in working with researchers to combat illegal activity by competitors.In addition, these audio recordings offer a new way to eavesdrop on wild seabird behavior. For example, the petrel’s recordings captured distinct landing and takeoff sequences previously observed in albatrosses, opening a new avenue of research into the flight patterns of this species. The recordings also highlight how human activity has upended food webs, as seabirds have become dependent on fishing vessel waste as a major source of food. “One of the advantages of this is that we can understand in a more unbiased way how much [seabirds] actually interact with vessels—every day, multiple times a day for all the species we looked at actually, which is crazy if you think about it,” Rutter said. “They're going out every day and just visiting boats all the time, and that shows the impact that we have on them as humans is really changing their feeding ecology,” he concluded.

item.content:encoded: Some customers have raised concerns about Backblaze's privacy policy taking effect next month, which says the backup and cloud storage company may sell certain personal information to advertisers.Backblaze’s current privacy policy says that in addition to the personal information that users may provide, such as their email address when creating an account, it may also “automatically” collect information, such as “your software, the operating system you use when accessing our service, your Internet Protocol address, and the date and time of each request you make to Backblaze.”The current policy adds: “Under no circumstances do we rent, trade, or share your address or e-mail address with any other company for their marketing purposes without your consent.” It also makes no mention of advertisers.

item.title: Huawei Is Guilty of Conspiracy To Steal Trade Secrets, a US Jury Finds
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
The Associated Press reports:
A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiring to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks as it grew into one of the world's biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks. But jurors acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy, a result that the company's lawyer said was a "profound rejection" of the government's narrative that it was corrupt from top to bottom and had a corporate culture of cheating, stealing and lying. Prosecutors had used the charge, commonly found in organized crime and drug cases, to accuse Huawei of operating illicitly to poach intellectual property and technological secrets from competitors and partners.
The convictions covered allegations that the company did business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions — including Iran and North Korea — and made false statements to U.S. government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds. In all, Huawei was convicted on 10 of 12 counts. The case in Brooklyn federal court involved no human defendants, but the company could be made to pay billions of dollars in penalties when it is sentenced next September...
Chinese officials said the U.S. has engaged in "economic bullying" and improperly used national security as a pretext for oppressing Chinese companies.
